title: Coriolanus
author: William Shakespeare
openingText: [A company of mutinous Citizens enters, carrying staves, clubs, and other weapons.]
about:
Caius Martius is a Roman patrician general who has spent his life on campaign and detests the common people of Rome. When the Volscian city of Corioles falls to him almost single-handed, the Senate honours him with the surname Coriolanus and proposes him for consul. The custom requires him to stand in the marketplace, show his wounds, and ask the citizens for their voices. He cannot bear it. Two populist tribunes turn the crowd against him; he insults the people in return; he is banished from Rome.

Coriolanus walks out of Rome and goes straight to his enemy, the Volscian general Aufidius. He offers Aufidius his throat or his service; Aufidius takes the service. The two of them march on Rome. The Romans send envoys to plead with him: an old patrician, his closest friend, and finally his mother. Volumnia, his mother, kneels in front of him with his wife and son and changes his mind. He calls off the attack. He returns to the Volscians, who kill him for the betrayal.

Shakespeare wrote Coriolanus around 1608, drawing on Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus. It is the last of his tragedies and one of his least often performed: a play of public arguments and political procedures, with a hero almost no audience has ever found easy to like. T. S. Eliot called it Shakespeare's most assured artistic success. The twentieth century made it his most politically charged.

angleCards.title: A hero who hates the public.
angleCards.text: Coriolanus is the Shakespeare hero who most despises the people he is supposed to serve. The play does not soften him. Watch what Shakespeare does with a tragic figure built for the audience to flinch from.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Coriolanus as Shakespeare's hardest case — a tragic hero who openly despises the common people — and see how the play handles a figure built for the audience to dislike.

angleCards.title: Mother and son.
angleCards.text: Volumnia, Coriolanus's mother, made him what he is. She is the only person in the play with any real power over him, and in the central scene she uses it. Some critics think she is the play's real protagonist.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the relationship between Coriolanus and his mother Volumnia, and decide what the play is finally saying about who shaped him and who, in the end, decides his fate.

angleCards.title: Politics as procedure.
angleCards.text: Half the play is set in the streets and forum of Rome, with tribunes, citizens, ceremonies of showing wounds, and the formal vote of consent. It is Shakespeare's most procedurally political play.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Coriolanus as Shakespeare's most procedural political play — the tribunes, the wound-showing, the popular voice — and see what it says about the mechanics of consent.

angleCards.title: Aufidius.
angleCards.text: Aufidius, the Volscian general, has fought Coriolanus a dozen times and lost. He receives him, makes use of him, and finally has him killed. He is one of Shakespeare's most interesting secondary villains.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Aufidius — Coriolanus's rival, host, and finally his killer — as the play's mirror to its hero, and see what Shakespeare does with the two of them.

cast.name: Caius Martius Coriolanus
cast.description: A patrician soldier who has spent his life fighting for Rome and despises the Roman commons for not appreciating it. He cannot ask for anything. He cannot lie about himself. He is one of Shakespeare's most uncompromising creations and one of his hardest to act.

cast.name: Volumnia
cast.description: The Roman matron who raised Coriolanus to be exactly what he is — a warrior, contemptuous of common men, incapable of compromise. She is also the only person who can make him change his mind, and in the play's climactic scene she does.

cast.name: Menenius Agrippa
cast.description: An older senator and Coriolanus's closest political friend, the patrician who tries to soothe the people with the parable of the belly. Witty, conservative, devoted. He tries to talk Coriolanus through the political crisis and is humiliated for his trouble.

cast.name: Sicinius and Brutus
cast.description: Two newly appointed tribunes of the plebs, the play's populist opponents. They work the crowd, manoeuvre Coriolanus into losing his temper in public, and engineer his banishment. Shakespeare gives them more political competence than he gives most of the patricians.

cast.name: Tullus Aufidius
cast.description: The Volscian commander who has been fighting Coriolanus for years and losing. When Coriolanus arrives in his house in exile, Aufidius embraces him as an equal, then gradually decides he cannot survive sharing the stage with him.

cast.name: Virgilia
cast.description: Coriolanus's quiet wife, who speaks very little in the play and whose silence has been read by every generation differently. In the final scene she is brought with Volumnia to plead for Rome, and her silent grief is part of what breaks her husband.

acclaim.quote: Coriolanus is Shakespeare's most assured artistic success.
acclaim.context: Hamlet and His Problems, in The Sacred Wood, 1920

acclaim.quote: The play of Coriolanus is to my mind one of the most amusing of our author's performances.

whyItMatters.title: A Tragic Hero Designed to Repel
whyItMatters.body: Coriolanus is the Shakespeare tragedy that most refuses to flatter its audience. Where Hamlet is sympathetic by being articulate and Lear is sympathetic by being ruined, Coriolanus stays sympathetic to almost no one. He calls the commoners 'curs,' 'fragments,' 'scabs,' 'cowards' — and means it, all five acts. He refuses, on principle, the small political performance that would let him be consul. He goes over to the enemy because he cannot endure home. He turns back from the attack on Rome and dies because his mother kneels and he cannot live with the choice either way. Shakespeare is doing something none of the other tragedies do: he is asking what to make of a man who would rather be honest than live, and who is honest about beliefs we want him not to have. It is the play that scholars and directors fight over most, because the same Coriolanus has been claimed across the political spectrum: Brecht read him one way, the Fascist regimes another, modern directors a third. The play resists each reading because the central figure is unbending. He is what he is. The tragedy is that what he is cannot live in Rome.

whyItMatters.title: The Most Political Play
whyItMatters.body: Coriolanus is the only Shakespeare play where the central action of two whole acts is parliamentary procedure. The Senate votes; the tribunes confer; the citizens debate in the streets; Coriolanus is required by custom to stand in the marketplace wearing the gown of humility and show the people his wounds. The play stages a constitutional question — what does Rome owe its commons, what does the army owe Rome, what is the relationship between popular consent and patrician honour — and refuses to settle it. Shakespeare is unusual enough in writing about politics at all; he is more unusual still in writing about politics this slowly, this carefully, this technically. There are no battles inside Rome after Act 1. There are votes, motions, manipulations, mob scenes, and a long argument about whether a great soldier owes the city anything beyond his sword. The play has been read as a critique of populism, of patrician arrogance, of the very institution of Roman government, and of all three at once. It is the play in Shakespeare where political philosophy is the action.

whyItMatters.title: The Scene with His Mother
whyItMatters.body: Act 5, Scene 3 is one of Shakespeare's most quietly devastating scenes. Coriolanus is camped outside Rome at the head of a Volscian army that will burn the city in the morning. Three deputations have come to beg him to spare it. He has refused all three. His mother Volumnia walks into his tent leading his wife Virgilia by one hand and his small son by the other, and asks him, in front of his Volscian allies, to make peace. She kneels in front of him. So does his son. He breaks. He gives the order to turn back. The scene is staged as a private family transaction held in public, with the audience watching and Aufidius watching and the Volscian army a few yards off — and what breaks Coriolanus is not the kneeling but the long silence after it, in which Shakespeare gives him no soliloquy and no asides, only the stage direction 'Holds her by the hand, silent.' The most articulate, most uncompromising hero in the canon is reduced to wordlessness by the mother who made him. He says, with full awareness, that the peace will get him killed. He gives it anyway. Then the play kills him, in the Volscian capital, almost as soon as he gets there.
